title: Landing Distance Over a 50 Ft Obstacle
conditions: Wing flaps 27°, paved/level/dry runway, maximum braking effort, approach speed = 90 MPH IAS

exampleCheck.note: Worked example printed on the chart (points A-F). Re-measured directly from reference/fig5-16-landing-distance-50ft.png pixel positions on 2026-10-01. Like fig5-15, the stored pressure altitude and weight were both wrong, not just the chart-reading target and curve data: point A's traced curve (t0~2037, matched to within 0.2% against an independently-labeled '2000 ft' curve trace) is the 2000 ft curve, not the originally assumed 6000 ft; and point C (weight correction) lands at pixel x~482, which calibrates to ~3200 lb, not 3100 lb (visually confirmed sitting almost exactly on the '32' weight gridline). OAT (65 F) confirmed correct. A follow-up check found the wind input was ALSO wrong: point F sits almost exactly on the '30' gridline in the headwind panel, not '10' as previously claimed -- the same wind=30 pattern independently confirmed on fig5-06, fig5-07, fig5-08, and fig5-15, suggesting all five ladder charts' worked examples use 30 mph headwind. weightExponent and windKPerMph refit from directly-measured B/D/F points (2230/2060/1700) with windMph=30. Model reproduces the chart's worked example to within 0.01%. NOTE: because the old altitudeCurves values here were also substantially wrong (e.g. old '6000' entry 1650/2750 vs. the now-independently-measured real 6000 entry of 2269/2670), all five entries were redigitized from scratch this pass, not just patched.

unverifiedAltitudes.note: Only the 2000 ft entry (above) is anchored to the worked example and independently verified to ~0% error. The 0/4000/6000/8000 ft entries were re-traced from the source chart using a shorter pixel baseline (two trace points ~85px apart, then extrapolated out to t0 and t120) and cross-checked by visually confirming each curve against its printed altitude label (see the overlay check performed during this pass), but are not confirmed against an independent worked example the way 2000 ft is. Medium confidence, not exact -- a clear improvement on the prior (unverified-guess) values, but extrapolation error grows at the temperature extremes.
